sources.title: AIS Aids To Navigations (ATONs)
sources.snippet:
AIS transmitters enhance navigation safety by broadcasting precise position and identification details from fixed or floating Aids to Navigation (AtoNs), such as buoys, beacons, or lights. This AIS data allows mariners to confirm their vessel’s position, recognize navigational aids well before they're visible visually or by radar, and plan maneuvers accordingly.

### Types of AIS AtoNs

There are three distinct types of AIS-equipped AtoNs, each with specific applications: [...] Real AIS AtoN  
A physical aid to navigation equipped with its own AIS transmitter that broadcasts its exact location and identification directly.

Synthetic AIS AtoN  
A physical navigational aid without its own transmitter. AIS messages for these aids are broadcast remotely from a land-based station, accurately representing the aid's location on electronic navigation systems. [...] Virtual AIS AtoN  
A navigational marker that exists only digitally through AIS broadcasts, with no physical structure. Virtual AIS AtoNs are ideal for temporary marking of hazards, seasonal buoy placements (e.g., ice-prone waters), or newly discovered dangers. They appear exclusively on electronic chart displays (ECDIS) or AIS-enabled navigational screens.

AIS AtoNs are clearly depicted on NOAA nautical charts using a magenta circle around the traditional AtoN symbol:

Used to measure advertising and show you more relevant ads. [...] Most sailors already know the value of the Automated Identification System, or AIS, and how it helps prevent collisions at sea. Some buoys and beacons are also equipped with AIS transmitters which give the position, description, and purpose of the aid. Three types of aids to navigation (ATON) use AIS.  
  
Physical AIS Aids [...] Virtual AIS aids might be used where buoys are moved seasonally, such as in sea ice, or where a marker needs to mark a new isolated danger or wreck, and there is not enough time for a ship to respond to install an actual physical aid to mark the danger. Virtual buoys and beacons are labeled ‘V-AIS' on an electronic display screen.
